# The complete diagonal-envelope deficit theorem

## Definitions and theorem

Fix an integer d>=2. Define

    t=1/(d+1),       Gamma=(d/(d+1))^d.

For a>0 and 0<=beta<=at, and every nonnegative integer h, put

    r_h=(1-ah)_+,       q_h=t-beta h,       p_h=t+beta(h+1).

Here x_+=max{x,0}. Define the envelope, only where it will be used, by

    E_d(q,r)=d^d q^(d-1)(r-dq)_+    for r>0 and q>0,
    E_d(q,0)=0                     for arbitrary real q.

The exact diagonal-envelope deficit is the finite sum

    D_d(a,beta)=Gamma sum_(h>=0) r_h^d
                   -sum_(h>=0)[E_d(q_h,r_h)+E_d(p_h,r_h)].       (1)

Every positive-radius term has q_h>=t r_h>0 and p_h>0, so the
definition never evaluates a positive-radius envelope at a
nonpositive threshold. No convention for a negative base to an
arbitrary power is needed.

For each integer 1<=H<=d, define

    a_H=(H+1)/[H(d+1)],       beta_H=1/[d(d+1)],
    W_(d,H)=sum_(j>=0)(1-a_H j)_+^d,
    K_(d,H)=sum_(j=0)^(H-1)(1-j/d)^(d-1)(1-j/H).

**Theorem.** The unrestricted maximum in (1) is attained. It has
the exact finite representation

    max_{a>0, 0<=beta<=at} D_d(a,beta)
       =Gamma max_{1<=H<=d}[W_(d,H)-K_(d,H)].                    (2)

In particular,

    0 < max_{a>0, 0<=beta<=at} D_d(a,beta) < Gamma/6.             (3)

Equivalently, throughout this full hard-tilt parameter domain,

    sum_(h>=0)[E_d(q_h,r_h)+E_d(p_h,r_h)]
       > Gamma sum_(h>=0) r_h^d-Gamma/6.                        (4)

The constant Gamma/6 is a sufficient uniform loss bound. This
theorem does not assert that H=1 maximizes the finite list in (2),
and does not identify the sharp universal loss.

## Complete dependency graph

The following are proved scalar lemmas, not hypotheses or
conjectural reductions. Each source contains its proof. The arrows
record every non-elementary dependency of the present theorem.

1. `candidate 31c8bae81eb26cc3` proves the
   rational continuous-kernel inequality (5) below. Its only named
   algebraic input is Descartes' rule of signs. the contributor and coherent
   independent audits are `unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)` and
   `unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)`.
2. Lemma 1 feeds both the uniform small-slope exclusion in
   `candidate c21aa22115d69526` and the
   positive-right-index estimate in
   `candidate 08dc040bda1a0f7a`.
   The independent escape audit is
   `unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)`.
   The knot audits are `unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)`
   and `unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)`.
3. `candidate a38c69b78fd106d1`
   proves the compact variational reduction independently of any
   proposed knot bound. Its independent audit is
   `unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)`.
4. `candidate a46be036ec7c0eb5`
   proves the complete J=0 estimate by elementary monotonicity and
   exact finite rational arithmetic. It is independent of Lemma 1
   and of the positive-J estimate.
5. The attained compact reduction, small-slope exclusion,
   positive-J negativity, and J=0 bound imply (2)--(4) by the full
   assembly proof below.

Thus there is no dependency on a mixed-integer center theorem,
localization conjecture, rounding lemma, simplex-normal extremal
classification, or numerical optimization. The only objects in
this graph are explicit one- and two-parameter scalar expressions.

## The proved scalar inputs, with exact constants

### Lemma 1: uniform continuous gain

Let theta=d/(d+1), and set
f(v)=(1+v)^(d+1)/(1+theta v)^d. For 0<=v<=1,

    f(v)+f(-v)>=2+theta v^2+(theta/4)v^4.                         (5)

All denominators are positive, including at v=1. One direct proof
uses the rational minorant

    g(z)=1+(1+theta)z+theta z^2/[2(1+cz+ez^2)],
    c=(2d+1)/[3(d+1)],       e=(d-1)/[6(d+1)].

The cited source proves f(z)>=g(z) for z>=-1 by clearing its
positive denominator. The resulting polynomial in x=1+z has a
fourfold zero at x=1 and at most four coefficient sign changes;
its positive constant coefficient and Descartes' rule therefore
give positivity away from x=1. Then the exact identity

    g(v)+g(-v)-2-theta v^2
      =theta v^4[1/4+e^2(1-v^2)]/
                  [(1+ev^2)^2-c^2v^2]

proves (5), because the denominator lies in (0,1]. The source
displays the cleared polynomial, its coefficients, and the full
sign argument; there is no dimension-dependent root conjecture.

### Lemma 2: the entire small-slope edge is negative

For each fixed d>=2,

    limsup_{a down to 0, 0<=beta<=at} D_d(a,beta)<=-Gamma/2.       (6)

This is simultaneous in a and beta, not a fixed-ratio limit.
For clarity, its mechanism is recorded here. Write v=beta/(at)
and define compactly supported kernels

    L_v(x)=(1-vx)^(d-1)[1-(d+1-dv)x]_+,
    R_(a,v)(x)=(1+av+vx)^(d-1)
                              [1-dav-(d+1+dv)x]_+.

Each formula is set to zero beyond its indicated support. On that
support its first factor is nonnegative. Their samples at x=ah
are the normalized envelope terms in (1). Their derivatives have
uniformly bounded variation for 0<=a<=1/(2d), 0<=v<=1. The exact
trapezoid identity with its signed endpoint correction is

    sum_(h>=0) g(ah)=(1/a)integral g+g(0)/2+E,
    |E|<=(a/8) Var(g').

The right integral is a finite polynomial expression with bounded
first and second derivatives in a on that rectangle. Consequently

    D_d(a,atv)/Gamma=-G_d(v)/a-J_d(v)-1/2+O_d(a),                (7)

uniformly in v. Here J_d is continuous, J_d(0)=0, and (5) gives

    G_d(v)>=v^2/[4(d+1)].

Given any sequence a->0, take a subsequence with convergent v.
If its limit is positive, the first term in (7) forces the
deficit to minus infinity. If v->0, discard that nonpositive term
and use J_d(v)->0; the upper limit is at most -1/2. This proves
(6) and retains all phase effects of the discrete sampling and the
extra right shift beta. The cited source proves each quadrature
identity and uniform derivative bound, and also supplies an
explicit positive cutoff if desired.

In particular, for some epsilon_d>0,

    D_d(a,beta)<0   whenever 0<a<=epsilon_d and 0<=beta<=at.      (8)

### Lemma 3: compact double-knot reduction

Fix 0<epsilon<=1. On

    epsilon<=a<=1,       0<=beta<=at,

D_d is continuous, its maximum is attained, and that maximum is
bounded above by the maximum of zero, the edge a=epsilon, and its
values at the finitely many admissible double knots

    a=t(H+J+1)/[H(2J+1)],
    beta=t(H-J)/[d H(2J+1)],                            (9)

where H>=1 and J>=0 are integers satisfying

    J<=H,       H<=(2d+1)J+d.                         (10)

Only knots lying in the compact parameter domain need be retained.
The proof first uses convexity in a between the envelope
activation lines. On either activation line, the mass minus its
same-side envelope is convex, and the other active envelope is
concave between its own activations. This moves a maximum to an
intersection or an outer edge. The reduced Hessian whose
positivity is needed is

    Gamma*d*(1+x/d)^(d-2)-(d-2)x>0,      0<=x<=1.

At x=1 its exact value is (3d+2)/(d+1)^2; its ratio comparison
proves positivity everywhere. The cited source explicitly treats
both types of activation line and all zero-threshold limits.

The outer edges beta=0, beta=at, and a=1 all have D_d<=0. The
edge a=epsilon is retained, and is not suppressed by the reduction.
The constant and pure-power mass functions are continuous when a
radius becomes zero, so mass-zero knots do not invalidate the
convexity or continuity argument.

### Lemma 4: all positive right indices have negative deficit

At every knot (9)--(10) with J>=1,

    D_d(a,beta)/Gamma <= -1/1080.                       (11)

This bound holds for every d>=2 and all admissible integer indices.
The source derives it from (5), exact trapezoid bounds, the finite
right-shift identity, and a fixed scalar rational function U(v).
It proves U(v)<=-1/1080 on [0,1] by three exact degree-six
Bernstein coefficient lists. Those lists are all displayed; the
estimate is not inferred from a sampled plot. In particular the
support endpoint is the integer sample J, so there is no discarded
partial cell or support-endpoint error.

### Lemma 5: the full zero-right-index family

At J=0 the admissibility conditions in (10) are exactly 1<=H<=d,
and (9) is exactly (a_H,beta_H). At these knots,

    D_d(a_H,beta_H)/Gamma=W_(d,H)-K_(d,H)<1/6.          (12)

For H=1, the bound follows by geometric summation with ratio
q=((d-1)/(d+1))^d<e^(-2)<1/7. For H>=2, scalar dimension
monotonicity gives

    W_(d,H)<=1/[1-(1-1/H)^H],
    K_(d,H)>1+(H-1)/(3H)
                    +sum_(j=2)^(H-1)(1-j/H)^H.

The exact rational comparison for H=2,...,9 is in the source.
For H>=10 it is enough to retain four terms:

    W_(d,H)<8/5,
    K_(d,H)>13/10+(4/5)^10+(7/10)^10,

giving a deficit below

    1643782927/10000000000
      =1/6-68651219/30000000000.

The source proves each real-variable monotonicity assertion used
to obtain these bounds. In particular, the zero rational margin
of its coarse H=2 table does not lose strictness, because the
lower bound on the j=1 kernel coefficient is strict.

## Full assembly proof

First dispose of a>=1. Only r_0=1 is positive. Its left envelope
is E_d(t,1)=Gamma, while the right envelope is nonnegative.
Therefore D_d(a,beta)<=0 for every such admissible pair, including
a=1 and arbitrary allowed beta. No other radius contributes a
boundary term.

There is a positive witness inside 0<a<1. Namely choose

    a=2/(d+1),       beta=1/[d(d+1)].

This is the knot H=1,J=0. It is admissible because d>=2. Its only
nonzero envelope term is the own left one, equal to Gamma, so

    D_d(a,beta)=Gamma sum_(h>=1)(1-2h/(d+1))_+^d>0.     (13)

Strict positivity follows already from h=1: d>=2 implies
1-2/(d+1)>0.

By (8), choose epsilon>0 small enough that all a<=epsilon have
negative deficit and epsilon<1/(2d). Then every zero-right-index
knot a_H satisfies a_H>=1/d>epsilon. The domain

    P_epsilon={(a,beta):epsilon<=a<=1, 0<=beta<=at}

is a nonempty compact triangle with one edge cut off. The finite
sum (1) is continuous there: only indices h<=1/epsilon can have
positive radius, each threshold is positive whenever that radius
is positive, and its envelope tends to zero whenever the radius
tends to zero. Thus D_d has an attained maximum M on P_epsilon.
The positive witness (13), after decreasing epsilon if necessary,
belongs to this domain and implies M>0. Values with a<epsilon or
a>=1 cannot exceed M, so M is also the unrestricted global maximum.
This proves attainment without assuming it in a variational step.

Apply Lemma 3 to this attained compact maximum. Its zero bound and
all three harmless outer edges are below M. Its a=epsilon edge is
negative by construction. Every knot with J>=1 is negative by
(11). Therefore the compact reduction bounds M above by the
maximum of the finitely many J=0 knot values. All these knots,
namely H=1,...,d, lie in the original admissible parameter domain,
so their maximum is also bounded above by M. These two inequalities
prove the equality (2), including that at least one such knot
attains the unrestricted maximum.

Every one of these d real values is strictly below Gamma/6 by
(12). A maximum of a finite set of numbers each strictly below
Gamma/6 is itself strictly below Gamma/6. Combining with (13)
gives (3), and rearrangement of (1) gives (4).

This completes the exact parameter-domain argument, including
attainment, all outer edges, the escaping edge, repeated or zero
sample endpoints, and strictness. No order of infinite sums and
limits was interchanged.

## Boundary and application scope

The theorem is stated for d>=2 because that is the scalar-kernel
range proved by the dependency graph. The one-dimensional affine
simplex case is covered separately, with zero deficit, by the
proved floor-counting theorem in
`candidate bbd9056fa863fc6b`; the
present theorem does not silently use a d=1 Padé or Hessian argument.
At d=0 this continuous-radius envelope is not defined and is not
needed.

The slope a=0 is not in (1): a constant infinite radius chain has
infinite mass. Its exclusion is principled, and (6) supplies exactly
the control required to approach it through finite positive-slope
chains. A finite constant chain must be treated by its original
finite fiber problem, not by substituting into this infinite-chain
definition.

The permitted tilt 0<=beta<=at is explicit. For actual simplex caps
the complementary range beta>=at is paid termwise by their ordinary
centroid bound; that geometric statement is separate from this
positive-threshold envelope theorem. Nor does (4) itself choose a
mixed-integer center, establish a low-maximum angular surplus, or
handle arbitrary convex fibers. Those are additional geometric
steps and are not inferred here.
